Content:

sections.normalized_html: Is the polygon shown above (a) simple or complex, and (b) convex or concave?
sections.readable_text:

Is the polygon shown above (a) simple or complex, and (b) convex or concave?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A polygon is convex if it has no internal angle larger than [MATH: 180^\circ.] In plain words, a convex polygon has no angles pointing inwards. Otherwise, the polygon is called concave.

A polygon is simple if its boundary does not intersect itself. Otherwise, the polygon is called complex.

In our case, the polygon is

  • [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{simple}}] since the boundary doesn't intersect itself, and

  • [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{concave}}] since it has an angle pointing inwards.

The shape below consists of [MATH: 6] line segments defined by the [MATH: 6] points [MATH: A], [MATH: B], [MATH: C], [MATH: D], [MATH: E], and [MATH: F.] These line segments form a loop.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3c3a0da8555d498ba11b8cabf3823fb5]

Content:
A chain of straight line segments that form a loop is called a polygon.

Content:
The line segments are the sides of the polygon, and the endpoints of the sides are the vertices.

Content:
For this polygon:

Content:
- The [MATH: 6] vertices are [MATH: A], [MATH: B], [MATH: C], [MATH: D], [MATH: E], and [MATH: F.]
- The [MATH: 6] sides are [MATH: \overline{AB}], [MATH: \overline{BC}], [MATH: \overline{CD}], [MATH: \overline{DE}], [MATH: \overline{EF}], and [MATH: \overline{AF}.]

Content:
To denote a particular polygon, we start at one vertex and loop around the polygon, reading off the vertices in order. So, the polygon above can be denoted [MATH: ABCDEF.]

Content:
The singular form of the word vertices is vertex. So, [MATH: A] is a vertex, [MATH: B] is a vertex, etc.

Item 2 — Tutorial: Naming Polygons

Content:
The name of a polygon is determined by the number of sides it has.

Content:
The polygon below has [MATH: 6] sides. A six-sided polygon is called a hexagon.

Graphic:

Content:

Content:

| [MATH: 4] | Quadrilateral |
| [MATH: 5] | Pentagon |
| [MATH: 6] | Hexagon |
| [MATH: 7] | Heptagon |

Item 6 — Tutorial: Types of Polygons

Content:
We can categorize polygons in different ways.

Content:
A polygon is simple if its boundary does not intersect itself. Otherwise, the polygon is complex.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/557b0c5adc92ec5855816264827a3006]

Content:
A polygon is convex if it has no angles pointing inwards. Otherwise, if the polygon has angles pointing inwards, we call it concave.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b0dbbad160a0b4dbf4c7a9345831ce90]

Content:
It might help to remember that a concave polygon looks a bit like the entrance to a cave when viewed from the outside.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5193ae62a3313243b9d8a2b3856948ff]

Content:
Note: A more technical way to define a convex polygon is to say that all of its internal angles are less than [MATH: 180^\circ.] If you're not sure what an internal angle is yet, don't worry! We'll learn more about the internal angles of a polygon in future lessons.

Item 7 — Example: Determining the Type of a Polygon

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/1f29f2a853b12f22bf3c7f92dae566f4]

Is the polygon shown above (a) simple or complex, and (b) convex or concave?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A polygon is convex if it has no internal angle larger than [MATH: 180^\circ.] In plain words, a convex polygon has no angles pointing inwards. Otherwise, the polygon is called concave.

A polygon is simple if its boundary does not intersect itself. Otherwise, the polygon is called complex.

In our case, the polygon is

- [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{simple}}] since the boundary doesn't intersect itself, and
- [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{concave}}] since it has an angle pointing inwards.

Item 10 — Tutorial: The Parts of a Polygon

Content:
Consider the pentagon [MATH: ABCDE,] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/89e78efde6945aa5b64e722ae7e49f06]

Content:
We have the following definitions:

Content:
- Two sides are adjacent (or consecutive) if they have a common vertex.

For example, [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.753,0.494,0.643}\overline{BC}] is adjacent to [MATH: \color[rgb]{0.902, 0.624, 0}\overline{AB}] and [MATH: {\color[rgb]{0.902, 0.624, 0}\overline{CD}}.]

[IMG: /graphics/17693d96d14395030c384b8f6fa137fe]
- Two vertices are adjacent if there is a side joining them.

For example, the vertex [MATH: E] is adjacent to the vertices [MATH: D] and [MATH: A].

[IMG: /graphics/4c8ccaf84e8329a8416da22e51bfdf14]
- A diagonal is a line segment that joins two non-adjacent vertices.

For example, [MATH: {\color[rgb]{0.902, 0.624, 0}{\overline{AC}}}, {\color[rgb]{0.902, 0.624, 0}{\overline{BD}}},] and [MATH: {\color[rgb]{0.902, 0.624, 0}{\overline{BE}}}] are diagonals of our pentagon.

Graphic:
